title: Pepper Vinegar Slaw
summary: The slaw that belongs on pulled pork: no mayo, a lot of pepper, vinegar that wakes the fat up.
story: Creamy slaw has its place, which is not on eastern Carolina pork. This is shredded cabbage in a hot vinegar dressing that pickles itself in the bowl. Make it an hour ahead so it wilts just enough, then keep it cold. It should crunch next to soft meat, not dissolve into the bun.

items: ½ head green cabbage, finely shredded

steps.title: Warm the dressing
steps.body: Heat vinegar, sugar, salt, peppers, and celery seed until the sugar dissolves. Whisk in the oil. It should taste too sharp in the pan — the cabbage will mute it.

steps.title: Pour and wait
steps.body: Toss with cabbage and scallions. Rest 30–60 minutes, tossing once. Drain a little if it throws too much liquid before serving.

proTips.text: Fine shred, not coleslaw-bag ribbons. The dressing has to coat, and a thick chip of cabbage just tastes like wet salad.
If you add mayo you have made a different slaw. That's fine. Don't call it Carolina.

milestones.label: Warm dressing
milestones.hint: Sugar dissolved, too sharp on purpose.

title: Texas Plate Ribs
summary: Dinosaur ribs: three bones of beef plate, salt, pepper, oak. The most impressive thing you can pull off a backyard pit.
story: Plate ribs are the short rib of the brisket world — huge bones, thick meat, a bark that looks like furniture. They do not need a sweet glaze. A Dalmatian rub, a hotter pit than a packer, and patience until a probe slides in between the bones. Serve them whole and let people fight over the last one.

items: 1 rack beef plate ribs (3-bone), 5–7 lb, membrane off
Beef tallow or water for a late spritz

steps.title: Trim the hard fat, keep the cap
steps.body: Peel the membrane on the bone side. Knock off only the hard, waxy fat on top. Leave a ¼-inch cap so the meat doesn't dry. Coat with salt and pepper on every surface, including the bones.

steps.title: Hotter than brisket
steps.body: 275°F, post oak, bone-side down. Plate ribs can take the heat. Leave them alone for 4 hours. Spritz only if the bark looks like it's turning to jerky.

steps.title: Don't wrap unless you have to
steps.body: Paper wrap after bark is mahogany if dinner is waiting. Otherwise ride them naked. Start probing between bones around 6–7 hours.

steps.title: Probe, rest, serve whole
steps.body: Done feels like brisket — warm butter, usually 200–205°F. Rest 45–60 minutes wrapped in a towel. Cut between bones. One bone is a meal.

proTips.text: If the bark is black and bitter, your fire was dirty, not too hot. Thin blue smoke or don't bother with plate ribs — they show every mistake.
Ask for plate ribs (chuck short ribs / dino ribs), not flanken and not English-cut braise ribs. You want the three long bones.

milestones.label: Bark set
milestones.hint: Mahogany, about 4 hours. Spritz only if dry.

title: Poor Man's Brisket
summary: A chuck roast smoked like a packer. Same bark, half the time, half the money, still a Texas plate.
story: Chuck has the marbling and connective tissue to eat like brisket if you treat it like one: Dalmatian rub, clean oak, wrap after bark, rest. It will not fool a Hill Country hall, but it will fool a weeknight table that wanted smoked beef without a 14-hour hostage situation.

steps.title: Season like brisket
steps.body: Pat dry. Salt, pepper, garlic on all sides. Overnight in the fridge if you can. Chuck has a lot of grain changes — glance at them now so you know how to slice later.

steps.title: Smoke to bark
steps.body: 250–275°F. 3–4 hours until the color is deep and the rub has tacked on. Spritz with water if the surface dries out.

steps.title: Paper wrap
steps.body: Wrap with a spoon of tallow if you have it. Back on until a probe slides in with almost no push, usually 200–203°F. Chuck can stall; don't panic at 165.

steps.title: Rest and slice against the grain
steps.body: Rest 45 minutes. Slice ¼-inch against the grain. If a piece shreds instead of slicing, you went past tender into pulled-beef territory — that's still dinner.

proTips.text: This is also how you make burnt-end-ish cubes without a packer. Cube after probe tender, glaze 30 minutes, done.
Choose a thick, even chuck, not a thin blade steak. You need mass or it dries before collagen gives up.

title: St. Louis Pork Steaks
finish: Fork-tender in the pan, not shoe leather on the grate
summary: Bone-in shoulder steaks, seared, sauced, and covered until they give. St. Louis backyard religion.
story: Pork steaks are cheap cuts from the shoulder, cut like a chop. In St. Louis they get a hard sear, then a swim in a pan of barbecue sauce with the lid on so the connective tissue melts. They are not a dry grill-mark flex. They should pull with a fork and taste like the sauce and the hog at the same time.

items: 6 pork steaks, ~¾–1 inch thick (from the Boston butt)
½ cup beer or apple juice

steps.title: Season and sear
steps.body: Salt and rub both sides. Hot two-zone fire. Sear 3–4 minutes a side over the coals until you have real color. Don't cook them through on the grate — they will seize.

steps.title: Into the pan
steps.body: Nestle the steaks in a foil pan or cast iron. Pour sauce, beer, Worcestershire, and butter around them. Cover tightly with foil.

steps.title: Braise on the cool side
steps.body: Lid the grill, 250–275°F, 60–90 minutes until a fork twists in the meat with no fight. Uncover last 10 minutes if you want the sauce to tack up.

steps.title: Rest in the liquor
steps.body: 10 minutes in the pan. Serve with extra sauce and cheap white bread to mop. This is not a tidy plate.

proTips.text: If you skip the covered pan you will serve grilled shoulder steaks that chew like a belt. The braise is the recipe.
Maverick's and similar cheap sauces are traditional. Save the fancy bottle for ribs.

milestones.label: Hard sear
milestones.hint: Color on both sides, not cooked through.

title: Applewood Pork Loin
finish: 140–145°F, then rest (it is not a shoulder)
summary: A lean roast that dries if you treat it like pulled pork. Pull it like a pork chop and let the rest finish it.
story: Loin is the cut people ruin on a smoker because the internet said 203°F. That number is for collagens. Loin is a big chop. Brine it, rub it, kiss it with apple wood, and get it off at 140. Sliced, it should be blushing and juicy. Sauce on the side — mustard or a thin KC.

items: 1 boneless pork loin, 3–4 lb, silver skin off
2 Tbsp kosher salt (or overnight brine: ¼ cup salt + ¼ cup brown sugar per quart water)

steps.title: Brine or dry-brine
steps.body: Overnight wet brine or a heavy salt the night before. Loin has no fat to hide dryness. Pat dry. Rub.

steps.title: Gentle fruitwood
steps.body: 250°F, apple or cherry. A 3–4 lb loin is often done in 90–150 minutes. Start probing at 75 minutes.

steps.title: Pull at 140
steps.body: Carryover will take it to 145. Rest 15 minutes. Slice ½-inch medallions. If you wait for 160 it will taste like a cafeteria.

proTips.text: A mustard-honey glaze in the last 15 minutes is allowed. A 3-hour wrap in foil is how you make pork-flavored sawdust.
Loin, not tenderloin. Tenderloin is smaller and even faster — 30–40 minutes. Don't mix them up.

milestones.label: Brine
milestones.hint: Overnight if you can. Pat dry, rub.

title: Cedar-Plank Salmon
wood: Alder or apple, plus a soaked cedar plank
finish: 125–130°F in the thickest part; pellicle set
summary: The fish cook barbecue people skip. Alder, a cedar plank, and the nerve to pull it when it's still silk.
story: Smoke is a seasoning on salmon, not a 12-hour identity. Dry the fillet until a pellicle forms, set it on a soaked cedar plank, and run a mild wood. Pull it when the thickest part is 125–130°F — it will flake and still look wet. Overcooked salmon is cat food with bark.

items: 1 side of salmon, 2–2½ lb, pin bones out, skin on

steps.title: Dry brine and pellicle
steps.body: Mix salt, sugar, pepper, zest. Coat the flesh. Fridge uncovered 45–90 minutes until the surface feels tacky, not wet. That tacky film is the pellicle — smoke sticks to it.

steps.title: Plank and mild smoke
steps.body: Fish on the soaked plank, 225–250°F, alder or apple. One chunk of wood is enough. 35–50 minutes depending on thickness.

steps.title: Pull early
steps.body: 125–130°F in the thickest part. The protein should just flake. Rest 5 minutes on the plank. Lemon, maybe a little white sauce or dill. Do not sauce it like ribs.

proTips.text: Hickory on salmon is a dare. If you can only burn hickory, use less and get it off faster.
If the plank catches fire you ran it too hot or didn't soak it. Keep a spray bottle. Char on the plank edges is fine; flames under the fish are not.

milestones.label: Pellicle
milestones.hint: Uncovered fridge until the surface is tacky.

title: Herb-Crusted Lamb Shoulder
finish: Probe tender, ~195–203°F, or 135°F if you want it sliceable and pink
summary: Shoulder treated like pork butt: herb, garlic, oak, until the blade gives. The cook that makes a table go quiet.
story: Lamb on a smoker scares people who only know chops. A shoulder has the fat and collagen to go low and slow. Garlic, rosemary, salt, and oak — not a mint jelly situation. Pull it to shred for pitas, or stop at 135 if you want rosy slices. Either way, rest it.

steps.body: Mash garlic, herbs, zest, oil, salt, and pepper into a paste. Score the fat cap in a crosshatch. Rub the paste into every crevice. Overnight if you can.
steps.title: Herb paste

steps.body: Fat cap up. 4–6 hours. Lamb fat can taste tallow-y if the fire is dirty — keep the smoke thin and blue.
steps.title: Oak at 275

steps.body: For slices: 135°F in the thickest part, rest 20 minutes. For pull: ride it to probe tender like a pork shoulder, around 200°F, rest 45 minutes, then shred off the blade.
steps.title: Choose your doneness

proTips.text: Lamb and mesquite is a bar fight. Oak or pecan. Save mesquite for a steak.
A sharp salsa or yogurt-garlic sauce on the side. Not a cup of mint jelly unless you are feeding your aunt on purpose.

milestones.hint: Overnight on the shoulder if you can.
milestones.label: Herb paste

milestones.hint: 135°F for pink slices, probe tender to pull.
milestones.label: Slice or shred

title: Dalmatian Rub
servings: About 1 cup — enough for a packer
summary: Salt and 16-mesh pepper. The Central Texas seasoning that is a philosophy, not a blend.
story: If the meat is good and the fire is clean, you do not need a fourteen-spice jar. Equal parts kosher salt and coarse black pepper by volume. Garlic if you are not arguing with a purist. Make it in a shaker, not a grinder — you want pebbles of pepper that become bark, not a grey dust.

items: ½ cup kosher salt (Diamond Crystal; ⅓ cup if Morton)

steps.title: Measure by volume, not vibes
steps.body: Pepper and salt 50/50 in a bowl. Whisk so the garlic, if using, disappears. It should look speckled like a Dalmatian — hence the name.

steps.title: Jar it
steps.body: A shaker with large holes, or a pint jar and your hands. Keeps months in a cupboard. Do not refrigerate — moisture clumps salt.

steps.title: How to use it
steps.body: Coat brisket, beef ribs, chuck, and sausage until you can barely see meat. Poultry wants a lighter coat. This is not a pork-rib candy rub.

proTips.text: Table pepper is too fine. It turns muddy and bitter over a 12-hour cook. Buy 16-mesh, or crack whole peppercorns coarse.
If your bark is salty, you used Morton at Diamond volume. Weigh it once, then you know your handful.

milestones.label: Jar
milestones.hint: Dry cupboard. Shake before every cook.

title: SPG House Rub
summary: Salt, pepper, garlic — the weeknight beef rub that still respects the meat.
story: SPG is what you reach for when Dalmatian feels too austere and a competition pork rub feels like dessert. Same coarse pepper, same salt, granulated garlic for the savory note that makes tri-tip and chuck taste finished. Keep a shaker by the pit.

steps.title: Whisk dry
steps.body: Combine in a bowl until the garlic no longer sits on top. Granulated garlic, not garlic salt — you already have salt.

steps.title: Use it
steps.body: Tri-tip, steaks, chuck, burgers, even potatoes. A heavy coat on beef, a dusting on chicken skin. Not for a 16-hour brisket if you want true Central Texas — use Dalmatian there.

proTips.text: Garlic burns if you sear screaming-hot after a thick coat. For steaks, SPG, rest 10 minutes, then sear. For low-and-slow, it just becomes bark.

milestones.label: Jar
milestones.hint: Label it so you don't grab the pork rub at 5 a.m.

title: Competition Pork Rub
finish: Brick-red, a little sweet, no clumps of brown sugar
summary: Paprika, brown sugar, chili — the rib and shoulder coat that turns into candy bark without tasting like a candle.
story: Pork can take sugar. Beef mostly cannot, not for 14 hours. This is the rub for ribs, pork steaks, belly burnt ends, and a Boston butt if you want a mahogany crust. Brown sugar is structural. Paprika is color. Cayenne is a rumor, not a dare.

items: ½ cup paprika (not smoked — you have a pit for that)
⅓ cup packed light brown sugar

steps.title: Break up the sugar
steps.body: If the brown sugar is clumped, rub it through your fingers first. Whisk everything until the color is even brick-red.

steps.title: Jar and date
steps.body: Keeps 2–3 months. Sugar draws moisture — if it turns into a brick, smash it and keep going.

steps.title: How to apply
steps.body: A thin binder of mustard or oil, then a coat you can still see meat through. Too heavy and it pastes, then slides. Second dust on ribs at the end for Memphis-adjacent dry.

proTips.text: Smoked paprika plus smoke is a double. Regular paprika lets the fire do the talking.
For a hotter cook (300°F chicken), cut the sugar by a third or it will scorch before the skin renders.

milestones.label: Jar
milestones.hint: Cool, dry. Smash if it cakes.

title: Coffee-Chile Beef Rub
summary: Espresso, ancho, brown sugar — a steak and burnt-end rub with a bitter edge that beef can handle.
story: Coffee on beef is not a gimmick if you keep it coarse and don't soak the meat in a latte. Fine espresso, ancho, a little sugar, salt, and pepper. It builds a dark crust on chuck, burnt ends, and a reverse-seared tri-tip. Too much on a 16-hour packer can taste like an ashtray. Use a lighter hand than Dalmatian.

items: ¼ cup finely ground espresso or dark coffee (not instant crystals if you can help it)

steps.title: Grind and whisk
steps.body: Coffee should be espresso-fine so it doesn't stay gritty on the crust. Whisk with the rest until even.

steps.title: Where it shines
steps.body: Chuck roast, burnt ends, tri-tip, a ribeye reverse sear. Dust, don't bury. Pair with a molasses glaze on cubes, not on a whole brisket.

proTips.text: Yesterday's coffee grounds from the percolator are stale and sour. Grind fresh or don't bother.

milestones.label: Dust, don't bury
milestones.hint: Beef that can take bitter. Not a 14-hour packer coat.

title: Lemon-Pepper Poultry Rub
summary: Salt, paprika, lemon zest, thyme. The bird rub that doesn't try to be pork candy.
story: Chicken and turkey want salt, a little sugar, herbs, and citrus — not a cup of brown sugar that never renders through the skin. This is the shaker for the Alabama white-sauce bird, competition thighs, and a holiday turkey. Lemon zest goes in dry; use it within a couple of weeks or skip the zest and add it fresh on the bird.

items: Zest of 2 lemons, dried on the counter 30 minutes

steps.title: Dry the zest
steps.body: Wet zest clumps the salt. Spread it 30 minutes, then whisk into the spices.

steps.title: Under the skin
steps.body: A little under turkey or chicken skin with butter, the rest on top. Thighs get a heavier coat than breasts.

proTips.text: If you dry-brine a turkey overnight with salt only, skip extra salt in this rub the next day or you will overshoot.

milestones.label: Mix and jar
milestones.hint: Use within a few weeks if you included zest.

title: Kansas City Molasses Sauce
finish: Thick enough to coat a spoon, shiny, not scorched
summary: Tomato, molasses, a little heat. The American default sauce, cooked so it tastes like a kitchen, not a bottle.
story: Kansas City sauce is thick, sweet, and tomato-forward. The trick is simmering long enough that raw ketchup and molasses stop tasting like the pantry. Vinegar keeps it from cloying. Use it as a late glaze, not a marinade, and never as a substitute for bark.

items: ½ cup molasses (not blackstrap unless you like bitter)
Optional: 1 tsp liquid smoke only if this is a stovetop-only batch with no pit

steps.title: Whisk cold, then heat
steps.body: Everything in a saucepan off heat until smooth. Then medium-low. Molasses scorches if you walk away.

steps.title: Simmer 20–30 minutes
steps.body: It should go from shiny-thin to a coat that clings to a spoon. Stir often. Taste: more vinegar if it's flabby, more cayenne if it's shy.

steps.title: Cool and jar
steps.body: It thickens in the fridge. Keeps 2 weeks. Thin with a splash of vinegar to glaze ribs; use it thick on burnt ends.

proTips.text: Glaze in the last 20 minutes. Sugar in this sauce will blacken if you mop it on at hour two.
If you must start from a grocery sauce, simmer it with vinegar and Worcestershire for 15 minutes. Straight from the bottle tastes like the factory.
